A study published in PLoS One in 2012 investigated the effects of targeted antiretroviral therapy on the depletion of gut T cells and the seeding of the HIV reservoir during acute HIV infection. The findings highlighted the critical role of early intervention in mitigating immune system damage and reducing the establishment of viral reservoirs. 2. Research by Wyl et al. in 2011 demonstrated that initiating antiretroviral therapy during primary HIV-1 infection leads to a temporary reduction in the viral set point after treatment interruption. This study, published in PLoS One, underscores the importance of timing in ART initiation for long-term viral control. 3. Hocqueloux et al. (2013) emphasized that long-term antiretroviral therapy initiated during primary HIV-1 infection is essential for achieving low HIV reservoir levels and maintaining normal T cell counts. This study, published in the Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy, highlights the benefits of early and sustained ART. 4. The ANRS VISCONTI Study, published in PLoS Pathogens in 2013, identified post-treatment HIV-1 controllers who achieved long-term virological remission after early initiation and subsequent interruption of antiretroviral therapy. This research provides insights into the potential for functional HIV cure strategies. 5. Steingrover et al. (2008) explored the dynamics of HIV-1 viral rebound following a single treatment interruption. The study, published in AIDS, found that the timing of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) initiation significantly influences rebound kinetics, emphasizing the importance of early treatment. 6. The Setpoint Study (ACTG A5217), published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2011, compared immediate versus deferred antiretroviral therapy in recently HIV-1-infected individuals. Immediate therapy was shown to impact the virologic set point positively, supporting early treatment initiation. 7. Buzon et al. (2011) presented findings at the Fifth International Workshop on HIV Persistence, showing that patients who initiated ART during primary infection experienced a reduced HIV-1 reservoir size after 10 years of suppressive therapy. This underscores the long-term benefits of early ART. 8. Grijsen et al. (2011) conducted a randomized controlled trial comparing no treatment with 24 or 60 weeks of temporary ART during primary HIV infection. Presented at the 18th Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI), the study highlighted the potential benefits of short-term ART in early infection. 9. Chéret et al. (2015) conducted a phase 3 trial (OPTIPRIM-ANRS 147) comparing intensive five-drug antiretroviral regimens with standard triple-drug therapy during primary HIV-1 infection. Published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, the study demonstrated the potential advantages of intensified regimens in early infection. 10. Schuetz et al. (2014) showed that initiating ART during early acute HIV infection preserves mucosal Th17 function and reverses HIV-related immune activation. Published in PLoS Pathogens, this study highlights the immunological benefits of early ART. 11. Wawer et al. (2005) analyzed HIV-1 transmission rates per coital act by infection stage in Rakai, Uganda. Published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases, the study revealed that acute-phase HIV infection is associated with significantly higher transmission rates, emphasizing the need for early detection and treatment. 12. Powers et al. (2011) used modeling to assess the role of acute and early HIV infection in the spread of HIV in Lilongwe, Malawi. Published in The Lancet, the study highlighted the critical importance of targeting early infection in transmission prevention strategies. 13. Carlson et al. (2014) investigated selection bias at the heterosexual HIV-1 transmission bottleneck. Published in Science, the study provided insights into the genetic and immunological factors influencing transmission dynamics. 14. Cohen et al. (2012) discussed the implications of early HIV infection for treatment-as-prevention strategies in a commentary published in PLoS Medicine. The authors debated whether early infection could compromise the effectiveness of such strategies. 15. Fonner et al. (2012) conducted a Cochrane review on voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) for changing HIV-related risk behavior in developing countries. The findings supported the role of VCT in reducing risky behaviors and improving HIV prevention. 16. Bellan et al. (2015) reassessed the infectivity of the acute phase of HIV-1 infection, accounting for heterogeneity and study design. Published in PLoS Medicine, the study used simulated cohorts to refine estimates of acute-phase transmission risk. 17. Pinkerton (2007) estimated the proportion of sexually acquired HIV infections in the USA attributable to acute-phase transmission. Published in AIDS, the study highlighted the significant role of acute-phase transmission in the epidemic. 18. Xiridou et al. (2004) examined primary HIV infection as a source of transmission among homosexual men in steady and casual partnerships. Published in AIDS, the study emphasized the importance of addressing primary infection in prevention efforts. 19. Coutinho et al. (2001) modeled the natural history of HIV infection and its epidemiological implications. Published in the Bulletin of Mathematical Biology, the study provided a framework for understanding disease progression and transmission dynamics. 20. Kretzschmar and Dietz (1998) explored the effects of pair formation and variable infectivity on the spread of infections without recovery. Published in Mathematical Biosciences, the study offered insights into the dynamics of HIV transmission. 21. Koopman et al. (1997) analyzed the role of early HIV infection in population-level transmission. Published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, the study highlighted the disproportionate impact of early infection on epidemic spread. 22. Pinkerton and Abramson (1996) used a Bernoulli-process model to assess the implications of increased infectivity during early-stage HIV infection. Published in Evaluation Review, the study emphasized the importance of early detection and intervention. 23. Jacquez et al. (1994) examined the role of primary infection in HIV epidemics among gay cohorts. Published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, the study underscored the need for targeted prevention during early infection. 24. Prabhu et al. (2009) updated estimates of sexually acquired HIV infections in the United States due to acute-phase transmission. Published in AIDS, the study reinforced the importance of addressing acute-phase transmission in prevention strategies. 25. Cohen et al. (2010) reviewed methods for detecting acute HIV infection. Published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases, the study highlighted the challenges and opportunities in identifying early infection stages. 26. Schackman et al. (2001) evaluated the cost-effectiveness of earlier ART initiation for uninsured HIV-infected adults. Published in the American Journal of Public Health, the study supported early treatment as a cost-effective strategy. 27. Priddy et al. (2007) investigated the detection of acute HIV infections in an urban counseling and testing population in the United States. Published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, the study emphasized the importance of acute infection detection in urban settings. These studies collectively underscore the critical importance of early detection, timely initiation of antiretroviral therapy, and targeted interventions in managing HIV infection and preventing its transmission.
